newsitem.title: CUBA: Vatican envoy pays homage to Cuban Felix Varela.
newsitem.headline: Vatican envoy pays homage to Cuban Felix Varela.

text.p: Vatican Foreign Minister Jean Louis Tauran, winding up a visit to communist-ruled Cuba, paid homage on Tuesday to the memory of Felix Varela, the 19th-century Cuban priest and nationalist who is a being considered by the Roman Catholic Church for sainthood.

Tauran laid flowers at Varela's tomb, which is located at Havana University. He told reporters afterward that Varela "was the father of Cuban culture and identity. He is today a man who unites all Cubans in the values of their nation".
Tauran refused to comment on his talks late on Monday with President Fidel Castro.

The Cuban news agency Prensa Latina said the meeting at the presidential palace took place in an atmosphere of respect, adding the two men exchanged opinions on areas of mutual interest. It gave no other details.

Varela, who died in 1853 and is one of the Roman Catholic figures most respected by Cuba's communist authorities, is considered to be a founder of Cuban identity. He was deported to the United States by Spanish King Ferdinand VII for promulgating a document calling for the abolition of slavery.
Roman Catholic Church officials last February began considering Varela for beatification, which is the first step on the road to being made a saint.

Castro's talks with Tauran, who is an archbishop and the first Vatican foreign minister invited to Cuba by the government, reflected improved relations between the Cuban authorities and the Roman Catholic Church, and could be the prelude to a meeting between Castro and Pope John Paul.
Castro is expected to meet the pontiff if he travels to Rome for a U.N. summit on food from Nov. 13 to 17.
If the meeting takes place, diplomatic sources said Castro would probably invite the pope to Cuba, the only country in Latin America he has not visited.

During his visit, which began last Friday, Tauran has called for more flexibility in granting visas to foreign priests and nuns to work in Cuba, giving the church access to the media and granting the church charity Caritas a wider field of work.

But Tauran has, at least in public, restricted his comments to the work of the church and has made no remarks about Cuba's political system. He has also pleased his hosts by condemning the longstanding U.S. embargo against Cuba.
Tauran, who also met Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina and parliamentary president Ricardo Alarcon as well as Cuban church leaders during his visit, was scheduled to leave Cuba later on Tuesday.
